title: The Sacred Atlas
subtitle: Every sacred site on Earth that depicts or worships a being with a PuniCodex temple — plotted, dated, and linked to its digital twin.
note: Coordinates are approximate monument centers. Deity identifications follow mainstream scholarship (UNESCO nominations, museum records, Assyriological and classical scholarship); contested or restricted identifications say so openly. Wikimedia Commons imagery is curated separately through the gallery curator and lands in each site's images array.

sites.name: Giza Pyramid Complex

deities.depiction: The king is buried as Osiris and rises as Ra — the Pyramid Texts, the world's oldest religious corpus, line the walls of Unas' pyramid.
The living king is Horus; the pyramid is his staircase to join the sun's circuit.

images.title: Giza Pyramids during "Forever is Now" exhibition

sources: Pyramid Texts of Unas, c. 2350 BCE
sites.summary: The last surviving wonder of the ancient world: the Fourth-Dynasty pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, aligned to the cardinal stars. Their temples and causeways map the dead king’s fusion with Osiris and his ascent to the solar circuit of Ra.

sites.name: Abu Simbel

deities.depiction: Ramses II enthroned between the falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty and Amun-Ra on the facade; the temple axis was engineered so sunlight reaches the sanctuary on the king's birthday.
Ra-Horakhty — Ra as the Horus of the horizon — anchors the facade colossi.

images.title: Templo de Ramsés II, Abu Simbel, Egipto, 2022-04-02, DD 26-28 HDR
Templo de Nefertari, Abu Simbel, Egipto, 2022-04-02, DD 153

sites.summary: Ramses II’s colossal rock temples in Nubia, engineered so that sunlight penetrates the sanctuary and illuminates the enthroned gods on the king’s birthday and coronation day — stone serving royal theology with astronomical precision.

sites.name: Karnak Temple Complex
sites.era: c. 2055 BCE – 100 CE, built over 2,000 years

deities.depiction: The Amun precinct — the largest religious complex ever built, grown by every dynasty for two millennia.
Amun-Ra: the hidden one becomes the visible sun; the Great Hypostyle Hall is his forest.

sources: Centre Franco-Égyptien d'Étude des Temples de Karnak
sites.summary: The largest religious complex ever built, grown over two millennia of pharaonic ambition. Its Hypostyle Hall and the Avenue of Sphinxes chart the rising power of Amun-Ra, king of the Theban pantheon.

sites.name: Luxor Temple

deities.depiction: The temple of the Opet festival, where Amun's barque procession renewed the king and the flood alike.

sites.summary: The southern half of Thebes’ living procession route, where the Opet festival re-enacted the divine birth of the king each year. Obelisks, colossi and the great colonnade remain a stone liturgy of Amun’s renewal.

sites.name: Valley of the Kings

deities.depiction: Every royal tomb is a machine for becoming Osiris: the Book of the Dead and Amduat maps of the underworld line the burial chambers.
anubis is worshipped at Valley of the Kings.

images.title: Thebes, Luxor, Egypt, Valley of the Kings from above
Thebes, Luxor, Egypt, Panoramic view of the Valley of the Kings

sites.summary: The hidden burial ground of the New Kingdom pharaohs, from Thutmose to Ramesses. Cut deep into the Theban hills, its painted corridors carry the Amduat and Book of the Dead — guidebooks for the sun’s nightly journey through the underworld.

sites.name: Dendera Temple Complex

deities.depiction: The Temple of Ḥwt-ḥr, Lady of the Sycamore — the best-preserved temple ceiling in Egypt, blue with Nut's body and the decans.

sites.summary: Home of the Temple of Hathor, whose zodiac ceiling and cryptic relief of the Dendera lightbulb continue to provoke debate. The goddess of music, love and the turquoise sky was worshipped here into Roman times.

sites.name: Temple of Edfu

deities.depiction: The House of Horus — the best-preserved temple in Egypt, where Horus of Behdet triumphed over Seth in the annual drama of the walls.

The Ptolemaic double temple where the northern sanctuary belonged to Sobek the crocodile — mummified crocodiles were found in its galleries — its nilometer and surgical relief making it the god's best-preserved house anywhere in Egypt.

The ritual center of the Kǒng lineage for over two millennia — the temple where emperors themselves performed rites to Kǒngzǐ, beside the cemetery where the Master and generations of his descendants lie; UNESCO World Heritage since 1994.

images.title: Edfu. Offerings gifts. Cartouches Ptolemy VIII

sources: Edfu Project, Akademie der Wissenschaften, Göttingen
sites.summary: The best-preserved temple in Egypt, dedicated to Horus the falcon, who here avenged his father Osiris. Its inscriptions are the most complete record of the ritual drama of the Egyptian temple.

sites.name: Philae — Temple of Isis

deities.depiction: The last temple of ancient Egypt, where Isis' cult outlived the empire and was still honoured in the 6th century CE; moved stone by stone above the flood.

sites.summary: The island temple of Isis, moved stone by stone above the Aswan High Dam. Inscriptions here preserve the last known hieroglyph (AD 394) and the last demotic graffito — the final breath of ancient Egyptian writing.

sites.name: Great Ziggurat of Ur

deities.depiction: The moon god Nanna's mountain — Ur's ziggurat, rebuilt by Saddam Hussein and conserved again after 2003.

images.title: Ancient ziggurat at Ali Air Base Iraq 2005

sites.summary: The Great Ziggurat of Ur-Nammu, raised c. 2100 BCE as a stairway between earth and heaven. Its restored mass is the surviving image of the Mesopotamian temple-mountain, the house where the god descended to receive the city’s king.

sites.name: Ishtar Gate, Babylon

deities.depiction: Nebuchadnezzar's processional way — glazed lions of Ishtar pacing toward her city's festivals.

images.title: Processional Way, Babylon - Google Art Project
images.artist: unknown artist Details on Google Art Project

sites.summary: The glazed-blue Processional Way of Babylon, flanked by bulls and mušḫussu dragons of Marduk and Ishtar’s lions. Through this gate the Babylonian New Year festival carried the gods’ statues to the Esagila, renewing the world’s order.

sites.name: Eanna Precinct, Uruk

deities.depiction: The Eanna — 'House of Heaven' — Inanna's precinct at the world's first city, where writing itself was born in her temple's accounts.
Inanna is Ištar's Sumerian name — one goddess, two languages.
gilgamesh is worshipped at Eanna Precinct, Uruk.
dumuzid is worshipped at Eanna Precinct, Uruk.

images.title: Columns with clay mosaic cones from the Eanna precinct in Uruk (southern Mesopotamia), Pergamon Museum, Berlin, Germany, unknown architect, 3600-3200 BC (01)
Columns with clay mosaic cones from the Eanna precinct in Uruk (southern Mesopotamia), Pergamon Museum, Berlin, Germany, unknown architect, 3600-3200 BC (03)

sites.summary: Eanna, the ‘House of Heaven’ of Inanna at Uruk — arguably the world’s first city and the stage of the Gilgamesh cycle. Here writing was invented for temple accounts, and the sacred marriage rite joined king to goddess.

sites.name: Eridu — Enki's Temple

deities.depiction: The Abzu — Enki/Ea's temple over the subterranean fresh-water deep. Sumerian tradition names Eridu's shrine the FIRST temple ever founded.

images.title: Painted pottery vessel (jug or ewer). From Eridu (Tell Abu Shahrain), Iraq. 3500-2800 BCE. Iraq Museum, Baghdad

sites.summary: The oldest temple sequence on earth: eighteen superimposed shrines of Enki, the god of the deep fresh waters and of wisdom. Sumerian tradition held that Eridu, rising from the abyss, was the first city to receive kingship from heaven.

sites.name: Nineveh — Ashurbanipal's Library

deities.depiction: The tablets of the Gilgameš epic slept here for two and a half millennia until Layard's dig — the first hero's afterlife began in this library.
The Ishtar temple of Nineveh stood beside the North Palace.

images.title: The Babylonian Campaign ,c. 704-681 BCE, Nineveh. Ashmolean Museum

sites.summary: The last capital of Assyria, where Ashurbanipal assembled the first great library. Its reliefs of lion hunts and its account of the Deluge — in the Epic of Gilgamesh — carry the flood story a millennium before Genesis was written down.

sites.name: The Parthenon

deities.depiction: Athena Parthenos — Phidias' thirty-foot gold and ivory statue stood where the treasury of an empire funded a goddess' house.

sites.summary: Pericles’ marble manifesto of Athena’s city: a temple, treasury and victory monument in one, housing Phidias’ colossal ivory-and-gold Athena Parthenos. Its sculpted frieze processed the Panathenaic sacrifice that renewed the goddess’s peplos.

sites.name: Delphi — Sanctuary of Apollo

deities.depiction: The omphalos — the navel of the world — and the Pythia's tripod, where Apollo spoke through the priestess.
The temple of Apóllōn, slayer of the Python; his oracle shaped the politics of the Greek world for a thousand years.
gaia is worshipped at Delphi — Sanctuary of Apollo.
The chasm that held the oracular spring before Apollo came: the great serpent Pýthōn guarded the rock, and the Pythia took her title from what the god's arrows killed here.

sites.summary: The omphalos — navel of the world — where Apollo’s Pythia spoke in verse and cities weighed their futures. Delphi’s oracle, sanctuary and games bound the Greek world into a single religious conversation.

sites.name: Olympia — Temple of Zeus

deities.depiction: Phidias' chryselephantine Zeus — seated, smiling, one of the Seven Wonders of the World; the games honoured him every four years.
The wooded Kronion rises above the great altar — Pausanias (5.7.10) records an altar of Krónos on the hill that still carries the Titan's name.

images.title: Edouard Manet - Olympia - Google Art Project 3
Edouard Manet - Olympia - Google Art ProjectFXD

sites.summary: The sanctuary of Zeus Olympios and birthplace of the Olympic Games. The chryselephantine Zeus by Phidias was reckoned one of the wonders of the world; the games were a truce of the gods across warring city-states.

sites.name: Delos

deities.depiction: The island of Apollo's birth — Leto delivered him here beneath the palm, and the whole island became his sanctuary, treasury and free port.
The island that anchored itself for a birth: beneath the palm in her sanctuary, Lētō bore Apóllōn and Ártemis, and the whole island became the god's treasury and free port.
delos is worshipped at Delos.

images.title: 20100706 Terrace of the Lions Delos Cyclades Greece

sites.summary: The tiny sacred island where Leto, pursued by Hera, bore Apollo and Artemis. Delos became the spiritual and commercial crossroads of the Hellenistic Aegean — the fixed point around which the Cyclades revolve.

sites.name: Epidaurus — Sanctuary of Asclepius

deities.depiction: The healing god's hospital-sanctuary — incubation halls, the snake, and a theatre with acoustics engineers still cite.
Hygíeia shared her father's healing city — inscriptions from the sanctuary give Health her own cult, altar, and votives beside Asklepios.

sites.summary: The sanctuary of Asclepius where healing was a sacred drama: incubation in the abaton, interpretation of dreams, and theatre as therapy. Its auditorium remains the acoustical marvel of the Greek world.

sites.name: Mycenae

deities.depiction: The citadel whose Linear B tablets first write the name of Zeus — a god three centuries older than Homer.

images.title: The entrance to the archaeological site of Mycenae on October 27, 2019
The Argolic Gulf from the archaeological site of Mycenae on October 27, 2019

sites.summary: The citadel of Agamemnon, ‘rich in gold’, with its Lion Gate and shaft-grave masks. Mycenaean bureaucracy wrote the Linear B tablets — the earliest Greek — and Homer’s Iliad made its kings the hinge between myth and history.

sites.name: Knossos

deities.depiction: The labyrinth's thread — the Ariadne whose ball of string tamed the Minotaur's maze beneath this palace.
theseus is worshipped at Knossos.

Knossos in Crete west court

sources: Arthur Evans excavations; Linear A/B archives
sites.summary: The palace of Minos and the labyrinth of the Minotaur: Minoan Crete’s administrative and ceremonial heart, its frescoed halls and store-rooms ruling a thalassocracy three and a half millennia old.

sites.name: The Pantheon

deities.depiction: The temple of all gods — its dome the vault of heaven, its oculus the sun itself; every god Rome met had a place in the sphere.

sites.summary: Hadrian’s temple to all the gods, whose un-reinforced concrete dome remains the largest of antiquity and the oculus its open eye to heaven. Re-consecrated as a church, it is Rome’s best-preserved interior and a model of cosmic architecture.

sites.name: Capitoline Temple (site)

deities.depiction: The Capitolium — Jupiter Optimus Maximus' temple that gave every capital city its name.

sites.summary: The Capitoline hill, Rome’s religious head: the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus Capitolinis stood here, where consuls sacrificed on taking office and generals offered triumphal spoils to the king of the Roman pantheon.

sites.name: Temple of Isis, Pompeii

deities.depiction: An Egyptian goddess in a Roman town — frescoed days before Vesuvius fell, showing Isis' cult as everyday Mediterranean religion.

images.title: Wall painting - idyllic landscape with sarcophagus of Osiris - Pompeii (VIII 7 28 - sanctuary of Isis - ekklesiasterion) - Napoli MAN 8570 - 01
Pompeii Temple of Isis with clouds

sites.summary: A Pompeian temple of Isis, rebuilt after the earthquake and entombed by Vesuvius in AD 79. Its frescoed initiation scenes show how an Egyptian goddess won the hearts of Roman townsfolk far from the Nile.

sites.name: Baalbek

deities.depiction: Baal of the Bekaa — the city kept its Canaanite storm god's name through three religions.
Rome's trilithon colossus: Jupiter Heliopolitanus, with Bacchus and Venus completing the triad.

sites.summary: The Heliopolis of the Roman East, where the Jupiter temple’s trilithon stones — among the largest ever quarried — and the exquisite temple of Bacchus stage the Baal-Hadad cult in its Greco-Roman afterlife.

sites.name: Jelling — The Conversion Stones
sites.deityNote: Harald Bluetooth's runestones — Denmark's baptism certificate. The pagan gods are notably absent: that absence is the monument's whole point.
sites.summary: The royal monuments of Gorm the Old and Harald Bluetooth: the runestones where Denmark proclaims its conversion to Christ while claiming the whole land — and a ship-setting that remembers the older north.

sites.name: Gamla Uppsala — The Temple Site

deities.depiction: Adam of Bremen (c. 1070) describes the temple: Thor enthroned centrally, flanked by Wodan and Fricco.
Wodan — Óðinn — with his warriors and birds.
Fricco — Freyr — with his priapus and peace; the great burial mounds stand beside the site.

images.title: Uppsala Mounds, Gamla Uppsala, Uppland, Sweden

sites.summary: The great heathen sanctuary of the Svear, where Adam of Bremen described a temple to Thor, Odin and Freyr and sacrifices recurred every ninth year. Under its three great mounds lay the kings of the Yngling line.

sites.name: Rök Runestone

deities.depiction: The longest runic inscription in stone — eight hundred years of scholarship later, its riddles still argue about Óðinn and the dead.

images.title: Rök runestone (Rök, Ödeshög Municipality, Östergötland, Sweden)

sites.summary: The Rök runestone — the longest runic inscription ever carved — is a ninth-century family monument that also preserves mythic catastrophe: Theodoric’s ride, the death of the sun, and riddles in verse.

sites.name: Newgrange — Brú na Bóinne

deities.depiction: Older than Stonehenge and the pyramids; later Irish myth made the great mound the síd of the Dagda, lord of the Tuatha Dé Danann.

images.title: Outer wall at Newgrange Passage Tomb - geograph.org.uk - 1932491

sites.summary: A passage-tomb older than Stonehenge and the pyramids: at the winter solstice sunrise, a beam of light creeps up its corridor and floods the chamber — a Neolithic engine for catching the turning sun.

sites.name: Hill of Tara

deities.depiction: The Hill of Kings — where Lugh's harvest games were played and Ireland's kings were inaugurated with the marriage of the land.

sites.summary: Teamhair na Rí — the Hill of Tara — seat of the High Kings of Ireland, where the Lia Fáil stood and the samhain fire of the gods was kindled. Its earthworks carry coronation drama across a thousand years.

sites.name: Avebury
sites.deityNote: A Neolithic henge older than any named god in this lexicon — the largest stone circle in Europe, its cult unnamed and unrecovered.

images.title: Avebury, Avebury Henge, Outer Stone Circle, North-east sector Wiltshire 1015546 20230817 0115
Avebury, Avebury Henge, Outer Stone Circle, South-east sector Wiltshire 1015546 20230817 0107

sources: UNESCO WHL 373 (Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites)
sites.summary: The largest stone circle in Europe, set within its own henge and village. Its avenues of sarsen stones once walked the faithful from sanctuary to sanctuary along the Ridgeway.

sites.name: Stonehenge
sites.deityNote: Built in stages over fifteen centuries. Every named deity attached to it in modern folklore is projection — the builders' gods are lost.

images.title: Stonehenge, Condado de Wiltshire, Inglaterra, 2014-08-12, DD 09

sites.summary: The most famous prehistoric monument on earth: concentric circles of sarsen and bluestone aligned on the solstices. Whether temple, observatory or ancestor shrine, it concentrated a landscape of the dead into a single engineered horizon.

sites.name: Kailasa Temple, Ellora Cave 16

deities.depiction: A mountain carved top-down out of a single basalt cliff — Śiva's home in the real world. The plinth carries the Rāvaṇa shaking-Kailāsa relief; shrine niches across the walls hold the whole pantheon.
meru is worshipped at Kailasa Temple, Ellora Cave 16.

images.title: Courtyard and Mahabharata Reliefs at the Kailasa Temple, Ellora 01
Small temple in side the Kailasa Temple, Ellora, cave (16)

sites.summary: The Kailasa temple at Ellora was not built but subtracted — a free-standing mountain carved top-down out of a single basalt cliff by the Rashtrakutas. It is Shiva’s Himalayan home reproduced in stone, and the largest monolithic structure ever cut.

sites.name: Elephanta Caves

deities.depiction: The Trimūrti — three faces of the Great Lord — carved into the island's basalt; Śiva as creator, preserver and destroyer in one six-metre head.

images.title: A seagull near Elephanta Caves, Mumbai

sites.summary: The island caves of Elephanta house the great three-headed Maheshmurti — Shiva as creator, preserver and destroyer in one colossal calm. Their sculptural theology taught the Puranic god to generations of pilgrims.

sites.name: Khajuraho

deities.depiction: The Kandariya Mahadeo — Śiva's marble mountain, its shikhara carved with eight hundred figures rising to the sky.

images.title: 20120303 zoophilia Lakshmana Temple Khajuraho India (panoramic version)

sites.summary: The Chandela temple city, where eighty-five spires once rose and twenty-five remain — sculptural mountain-ranges of the gods whose friezes join eros and asceticism in a single vision of divine fullness.

sites.name: Angkor Wat

deities.depiction: The largest religious monument on Earth — built as Viṣṇu's temple, its galleries a four-kilometre relief of the Churning of the Sea of Milk.

sites.summary: The largest religious monument ever built: Vishnu’s temple-mountain raised by Suryavarman II as his mausoleum and cosmic model. Its bas-reliefs process the Churning of the Sea of Milk around a full kilometre of gallery.

sites.name: Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur

deities.depiction: The Chola colossus — a vimana of granite crowned with a single eighty-tonne capstone, Śiva's house built to outlast the dynasty.

images.title: Brihadisvara Temple during Maha Shivaratri-WUS03611 (edit)

images.title: An elephant relief on the Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur

sites.summary: The Brihadeeswarar temple of Rajaraja Chola — the Great Living Chola Temple — whose 66-metre vimana crowned by a single carved stone still dominates the delta. Its inscriptions map an empire’s gifts to Shiva.

sites.name: Varanasi — Kashi Vishwanath

deities.depiction: Kāśī — the city founded to Śiva, where the ghats have burned with funeral fires for three thousand years without interruption.
ganga is worshipped at Varanasi — Kashi Vishwanath.

images.title: Scindia Ghat in morning, Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, India (2012)

sites.summary: Kashi, the city of light on Shiva’s trident: continuously inhabited for three millennia and the holiest place to die in Hindu cosmology. Its ghats stage the daily drama of cremation and liberation on the Ganges.

sites.name: Ramanathaswamy Temple, Rameswaram

deities.depiction: The island where Rāma worshipped Śiva before crossing to Laṅkā — the epic's bridge begins here.

sites.summary: The island temple at India’s southern threshold, where Rama worshipped Shiva before crossing to Lanka. Its corridors — among the longest of any Hindu temple — walk the pilgrim toward the lingam of Ramanathaswamy.

sites.name: Meenakshi Temple, Madurai

deities.depiction: Meenakshi — the fish-eyed goddess, a royal form of Pārvatī, who ruled Madurai and married Śiva in the temple's annual grand wedding.

images.title: Sri Meenakshi Devasthanam Temple from courtyard

sites.summary: The Meenakshi temple city, where the goddess rules as queen and Shiva as Sundareswarar her consort. Its thousand-pillared halls and gopuram statues make Madurai the living heart of Tamil bhakti.

sites.name: Konark Sun Temple

deities.depiction: The Sun's chariot of stone — twelve carved wheels, seven straining horses, Sūrya rising over the Bay of Bengal.

images.title: 13th Century sculptures at Konark Sun Temple Puri district, Odisha, India
13th Century stone curvings at Konark Sun Temple Puri district, Odisha, India

sites.summary: The Sun Temple conceived as Surya’s chariot: twenty-four carved wheels, seven straining horses, and friezes of courtly and cosmic life. The dawn strikes the deity through the eastern gate no more — the wheels remain.

sites.name: Borobudur

deities.depiction: A mandala you climb — two million blocks, ten terraces, and at the summit the great stupa; the central Buddha's identity is debated, with Mahāvairocana the leading reading.

sites.summary: The largest Buddhist monument on earth: a mandala in stone walked upward through ten levels of galleries — the pilgrim ascends from the world of desire to the formless. Its 2,672 relief panels are a complete illustrated sutra.

sites.name: Sanchi Stupa

deities.depiction: The Great Stupa — Ashoka raised it over the Buddha's relics; its toranas narrate the life in stone.

sites.summary: The Great Stupa of Ashoka, its hemispherical mound enclosing relics of the Buddha beneath four toranas carved with his life and past lives. Sanchi is the earliest surviving stone architecture of the Buddhist world.

sites.name: Mahabodhi Temple, Bodh Gaya

deities.depiction: The diamond throne beneath the Bodhi tree — the exact ground of the awakening, the holiest site in Buddhism.

images.title: Votive Stupas - Mahabodhi Temple Complex - Bodh Gaya (13)
Votive Stupas - Mahabodhi Temple Complex - Bodh Gaya (18)

sites.summary: The tree beneath which the Buddha awoke: the Mahabodhi temple marks the exact spot of enlightenment, with its diamond-throne shrine and descendant of the original bodhi tree — Buddhism’s holiest coordinate.

sites.name: Tōdai-ji, Nara

deities.depiction: The Daibutsu — Mahāvairocana in gilded bronze, the largest bronze Buddha ever cast when Emperor Shōmu raised it.

images.title: The Great Buddha Hall of Tōdai-ji, Nara, November 2016

sources: Shōsōin documents; UNESCO WHL 870 (Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara)
sites.summary: The Great Eastern Temple of Nara, whose Daibutsu — a 15-metre bronze Vairocana — was the largest cast figure on earth when consecrated in AD 752. Todaiji anchored Buddhism as the state religion of Japan.

sites.name: Kōtoku-in Daibutsu, Kamakura

deities.depiction: Amitābha in the open air — the hall that housed him was swept away by a tsunami in 1498, and the Buddha has sat outdoors ever since.

images.title: The Great Buddha of Kōtoku-in (Kamakura Daibutsu)

sites.summary: The Amida Buddha of Kōtoku-in, cast in bronze in AD 1252 and serene through tidal waves and earthquakes. After the hall washed away in 1498, the great figure has sat in the open air, roofed by the sky.

sites.name: Ise Jingū

deities.depiction: The shrine of the Sun Goddess — Amaterasu's mirror is one of the Three Treasures of the throne; the Shikinen Sengū renewal has kept carpenters in unbroken practice for thirteen centuries.
tsukuyomi is worshipped at Ise Jingū.

images.title: Ise-Grand-Shrine-Emperor-Meiji-Sadahide-Utagawa-1869
images.artist: Sadahide Utagawa (1807-1873), 歌川 貞秀

sources: Ise Shō Naike tradition; UNESCO (tentative list)
sites.summary: Ise Jingu, the shrine of Amaterasu and the imperial regalia: rebuilt identically every twenty years for over a millennium — the doctrine of tokowaka, that renewal itself is the permanent offering.

sites.name: Fushimi Inari Taisha

deities.depiction: Ten thousand vermilion torii climbing the mountain — the kami of rice, sake and success, foxes at every gate.

images.title: Torii path with lantern at Fushimi Inari Taisha Shrine, Kyoto, Japan

sites.summary: The mountain of the rice-god Inari, where some ten thousand vermilion torii form tunnels up the slopes. Each gate is a donor’s prayer; the fox-messengers watch the boundary between village and sacred height.

sites.name: Itsukushima Shrine

deities.depiction: The great torii standing in the tide — the shrine honours the three daughters of Susanō, the storm god.
benzaiten is worshipped at Itsukushima Shrine.

images.title: Main Shrine, Itsukushima Shinto Shrine, Miyajima, 20240816 1710 4026

sites.summary: The shrine that floats: Itsukushima’s great torii stands in the sea, and at high tide the whole complex — halls, corridors and stage — appears to sail. The island itself is the goddess, body and shrine one.

sites.name: Izumo Taisha

deities.depiction: The great shrine of Ōkuninushi, lord of the land who yielded it to Amaterasu's line in exchange for the shrine's rank — Japan's oldest recorded diplomatic settlement.

sites.summary: Izumo Taisha, where all the kami of Japan are said to gather each October (kannazuki, the ‘month without gods’ everywhere else). The shrine of ōkuninushi measures its ancient halls in giant shaku.

sites.name: Kasuga Taisha
sites.deityNote: The four clan kami of the Fujiwara ride here in annual procession; the Fujiwara kami are not yet in the lexicon.

images.title: Sacred Sugi inside Kasuga Taisha shrine

sources: UNESCO WHL 870 (Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara)
sites.summary: The Kasuga shrine of Nara, lantern-lit for a thousand years: two thousand stone lanterns in the forest and a thousand bronze before the shrines, lit twice a year for the festivals of the Fujiwara clan’s tutelary kami.

sites.name: Temple of Heaven

deities.depiction: tian is worshipped at Temple of Heaven.
shangdi is worshipped at Temple of Heaven.

sites.deityNote: The altar of Tiān — Heaven itself, unrepresented as image; the Son of Heaven prayed here for the harvest. The high god Di 帝, named on Shang oracle bones, is the deep ancestor of this rite.

images.title: Temple of Heaven, Beijing, China - 010 edit
Hall of Prayer for Good Harvest

sites.summary: The Circular Mound and Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, where the Son of Heaven fasted and offered to Heaven each winter solstice. Its geometry — round heaven on square earth, all in triple-eaved blue — is China’s cosmology in timber.

sites.name: White Cloud Temple

deities.depiction: The headquarters of the Complete Perfection order, where Lǎozī is honoured as Taishang Laojun — the Lord Lao Most High.

sites.summary: Baiyunguan, the White Cloud Temple: seat of the Quanzhen school of Taoism and the shrine of Qiu Chuji, the ‘Perfected’ who counselled Genghis Khan. Its monks still keep the Complete Perfection liturgy.

sites.name: Lingyin Temple — Feilai Feng

deities.depiction: The Peak that Flew from Afar — its cliffs carry Song-dynasty carvings of Guānyīn among the largest surviving stone bodhisattvas in China.

sites.summary: The Temple of the Soul’s Retreat, founded by the Indian monk Huili in AD 326: one of China’s wealthiest Buddhist foundations, its cliffs carved with hundreds of Song-period smiling Buddhas above the Feilai stream.

sites.name: Wudang Mountains

deities.depiction: The Perfected Warrior's mountain — Zhenwu, the dark lord of the north, subdued his serpent and tortoise here; the Ming emperor built the Golden Hall in his honour.

sites.summary: Wudang’s peaks are the cradle of Taijiquan and the sanctuaries of Zhenwu, the Perfected Warrior. Its cliff-hanging temples and gilded bronze hall crown five centuries of Ming imperial patronage.

sites.name: Mount Qingcheng

deities.depiction: The mist mountain where the Way of the Celestial Masters began — organized Taoism's birthplace in the shadow of Dujiangyan's waters.

The island mountain counted as Guānyīn's chief earthly abode in China — Potalaka of the Eastern Sea — with temples and a cave-shrine tradition of her manifestations reaching back to the Tang; one of the four sacred Buddhist mountains of China.

Mañjuśrī's bodhimaṇḍa — the five-peak mountain where the bodhisattva of wisdom is believed to dwell, and a Mahāyāna pilgrimage center since at least the Northern Wei; Xuanzang and the Tibetan sources alike place Wénshū here.
Dìzàng's mountain — the bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha's earthly seat since the ninth-century monk Dizang (Kṣitigarbha's incarnation) meditated here; one of China's four great Buddhist sacred mountains.
Samantabhadra's mountain — Pǔxián rides his six-tusked white elephant here above the sea of clouds; Buddhism's lamp on this peak has burned reportedly unbroken for a thousand years.

sources: UNESCO WHL 1001 (Mount Qingcheng and the Dujiangyan Irrigation System)
sites.summary: Mount Qingcheng, ‘green city wall’ — one of Taoism’s birthplaces, where Zhang Daoling received the Way of the Celestial Masters in the second century. Its mist-wrapped shrines still teach the oldest organised Taoist lineage.

sites.name: Naqsh-e Rostam

deities.depiction: Royal tombs cut into the cliff — every investiture scene shows the winged symbol of Ahura Mazdā hovering over the king; a fire altar burns below.

sites.summary: The royal necropolis of Persepolis’ kings: four colossal cruciform tombs of Darius and his heirs cut into the cliff, above the greatest relief of Sasanian Iran — Shapur I’s mounted triumph over two Roman emperors.

sites.name: Persepolis

deities.depiction: Every foundation inscription opens the same way — 'by the favour of Ahura Mazdā'. The apadana's tribute bearers walked past the faravahar of the Wise Lord.

sites.summary: The ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid world, where subject nations carved tribute processions up the Apadana stairs. Its columns and bull-capitals staged the empire’s order — Ahura Mazda’s light above a hundred peoples.

sites.name: Atash Behram of Yazd

deities.depiction: A sacred fire kept burning for centuries — the physical custody of the Wise Lord's truth.

sites.summary: The Atash Behram of Yazd — the highest grade of Zoroastrian fire-temple, its sacred flame tended continuously since AD 470. Behind the ochre walls of the old quarter, the world’s oldest prophetic religion still burns.

sites.name: Ugarit (Ras Shamra)

deities.depiction: The tablets of the Baal Cycle — the storm god's battle with Prince Sea was read here until the city burned.
The high god's marzeah — El, Father of Years, enthroned at the source of the rivers.
ꜥAnat's furious war-poem fills the gaps of the cycle; she waded in blood up to the knees.

sources: RS 3.322+ tablets; editio princeps by Virolleaud
sites.summary: The Syrian city where the cuneiform alphabet was forged c. 1400 BCE — the twenty-seven signs from which nearly every alphabet on earth descends. Its tablets preserve the Baal cycle, where the storm-god battles Sea and Death.

sites.name: Byblos

deities.depiction: The Lady of Byblos — Baalat Gebal, the city's mistress, kin to Astarte; her temple endured through five millennia of rebuilds.
adonis is worshipped at Byblos.

sites.summary: Continuously inhabited for seven millennia, Gebal gave the Greeks their word for book — biblos — through its papyrus trade. The city of El, high god of the Canaanite pantheon, and cradle of the first Phoenician letters.

sites.name: Carthage Tophet

deities.depiction: The precinct of Tanit and Baal Hammon — thousands of stelae to the Lady of Carthage; Tanit is not yet in the lexicon, Astarte's Punic daughter stands here.

sources: American Schools of Oriental Research excavations
sites.summary: The tophet of Carthage, where the city of Tanit and Baal Hammon kept its vows. The stelae fields — thousands of carved markers — remain the most debated evidence of Phoenician child sacrifice in the ancient sources.

sites.name: Tel Megiddo
sites.deityNote: Twenty-six layers of cult and war — Armageddon's tel. Canaanite temples stood here; the specific dedications are lost in the strata.
sites.summary: Thirty cities stacked on one tell above the Jezreel plain — the crossroads where the armies of Egypt, Assyria and Israel met. Its name became Greek Armageddon: the hill where tradition says the last battle will be fought.

sites.name: Yazılıkaya Rock Sanctuary

deities.depiction: The rock galleries' procession of gods — the Hittite pantheon carved in basalt relief, marching toward the storm god's embrace.
The sword-god of Chamber B — the Hittite storm god with his hieroglyphic name.

images.title: Painting of Hittite Rock Sanctuary at Yazilikaya (28626703061)
Relief of the Twelve Underworld Gods Chamber B Yazilikaya Hattusa

sites.summary: The rock sanctuary of the Hittite gods: a natural gallery where sixty-three deities process in relief — the storm-god Teshub and Hepat enthroned, the god-kings of Hattusa’s empire walking forever in stone.

sites.name: Hattusa — The Great Temple

deities.depiction: The storm god of Ḫatti's great temple in the Hittite capital, beside the archives that held 30,000 cuneiform tablets.

sites.summary: The mountain-ringed capital of the Hittite empire, city of a thousand gods. Its lion gates, great temple and archives of cuneiform tablets held the legal and ritual order of Anatolia’s first great power.

sites.name: Alaca Höyük
sites.deityNote: Hattian royal tombs at the sacred spring — the stratum beneath the Hittite stratum, before the Indo-European names arrived.
sites.summary: The royal tombs of the Hattian ancestors: thirteen shaft-graves with iron daggers and standards of bulls and stags — the ritual bronze horizon of Anatolia’s earliest kings, five centuries before Hattusa rose.

sites.name: Peryn — Perun's Island

deities.depiction: The Perun shrine of Novgorod — Vladimir's pantheon head before baptism; the idols were thrown down here in 988.

sites.summary: The sacred grove of Perun near Novgorod: the oak sanctuary of the thunder-god where Vladimir’s Rus made sacrifice before the baptism of 988. Excavated post-holes and offerings sketch the shrine of the Slavic Zeus.

sites.name: Arkona — Cape Arkona
sites.deityNote: Svantevit's temple-fortress stood on this cape until the Danes razed it in 1168, carrying the idol's head to Lund. Svantevit is not yet in the lexicon.
sites.summary: The fortified temple of Svantovit on Rügen island, where four-faced idols held the state oracle of the Rani Slavs — a horn of plenty, white horse and war-banner — until the Danes cast it into the sea in 1168.

sites.name: Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove

deities.depiction: Ọṣun's living grove on the river — shrines, sculptures and the goddess's annual festival, unbroken and UNESCO-listed.

images.title: First palace of the king osogbo at the osun-osogbo sacred grove

sites.summary: The sacred grove of Osun, the river goddess of fertility and sweet water: forest shrines, sculptured gates and the annual festival that walks the river’s course — Yoruba religion alive inside a protected wilderness.

sites.name: Ile-Ife

deities.depiction: The cradle city of the Yoruba — Odùduwà descended here and founded the line of kings; the naturalistic bronzes of Ife are among humanity's finest portrait sculpture.

images.title: Faculty of Medicine, Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, Osun State, Nigeria (12998041954)

sources: Ife corpus bronzes; British Museum/Ife Museum
sites.summary: Ilé-Ifẹ, the cradle of Yoruba civilisation, where Oduduwa descended and the world began. Its naturalistic bronze heads — cast with a sophistication Europe would not match for centuries — are the serene face of the orisha tradition.

sites.name: Templo Mayor, Tenochtitlan

deities.depiction: The double temple's north half — Tlāloc's altar with its blue-and-white paint still bright when Cortés arrived.
The south half — Huītzilōpōchtli's shrine, the hummingbird of war, rebuilt five times as the empire grew.

sources: UNESCO WHL 412 (Historic Centre of Mexico City)
sites.summary: The Great Temple of Tenochtitlan: the double pyramid where Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc received the sacrifices that fed the sun. Its excavated offertory cache — the Coyolxauhqui stone — is Aztec cosmology at full scale.

sites.name: Teotihuacan

deities.depiction: The Feathered Serpent's pyramid — two hundred sacrificed warriors cemented its foundations six hundred years before the Aztec named the city 'the place where the gods were born'.

sites.summary: The city where the gods were born: its Pyramid of the Sun and Moon aligned a metropolis of 125,000 — the largest city of the pre-Columbian Americas — and the Avenue of the Dead carried pilgrims between cosmic mountains.

sites.name: Great Pyramid of Cholula

deities.depiction: The largest pyramid on Earth by volume — Aztec legend held this was Quetzalcōātl's city before his departure east over the sea.

images.title: Gran Pirámide de Cholula, Puebla, México, 2013-10-12, DD 10
Gran Pirámide de Cholula, Puebla, México, 2013-10-12, DD 03

sites.summary: The Great Pyramid of Cholula — by volume the largest monument ever built — raised in superimposed temples of Quetzalcoatl across a thousand years. The Virgen de los Remedios crowns it where the feathered serpent once dwelt.

sites.name: Qorikancha, Cuzco

deities.depiction: The golden enclosure of the Sun — walls sheeted in gold that the conquistadors stripped within a year; the Dominican church stands inside its perfect masonry now.

images.title: Cusco Coricancha view1
images.artist: No machine-readable author provided. Xauxa assumed (based on copyright claims).

sites.summary: The golden enclosure of Cuzco: the Inca’s richest temple, its walls lined with gold and planted with maize of silver, dedicated to Inti the sun. The Santo Domingo convent was mortared directly onto its flawless masonry.

sites.name: Machu Picchu

deities.depiction: The Intihuatana — the hitching-post of the sun, where the priests tied the sun to the stone at solstice so it could not wander off.

sites.summary: The estate in the sky of Pachacuti, engineered between two fault lines with terraces, temples and an Intihuatana — the ‘hitching post of the sun’. Its stones fit without mortar, as mountains fit the sky.

sites.name: Sacsayhuamán
sites.deityNote: The thunderhead fortress above Cuzco — walls of stones fitted without mortar, the storm's seat above the city of the Sun.

images.title: Sacsayhuamán Décembre 2006 - Vue Panoramique - Pleine résolution

sites.summary: The cyclopean fortress above Cuzco, where zigzag walls of hundred-tonne stones frame the great plaza of Inti Raymi. Each year the sun-festival of the Inca still rises here on the winter solstice.

sites.name: Raqch'i — Temple of Viracocha

deities.depiction: The only great temple of Wiraqucha — the creator's house at the centre of the Inca road, its central wall two metres thick and forty metres long.

sites.summary: The temple of Viracocha at Raqchi: a soaring columned hall unique in Inca architecture, dedicated to the creator god whose single word made the world. Its agricultural terraces and storehouses fed the pilgrims’ road.

sites.name: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau

deities.depiction: The city of refuge — under Lono's law of sanctuary, anyone who reached these walls was absolved, whatever their crime.

images.title: Kiʻi at Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau (a0007729)
images.artist: This file was created by Thomas Tunsch. It is not in the public domain and use o

sites.summary: Pu‘uhonua o Hōnaunau — the Place of Refuge: breakers of kapu who reached its walls were absolved by priests of the taboo-god. The great temple platform and carved wooden gods mark Hawaii’s sanctuary law.

sites.name: Taputapuātea

deities.depiction: taaroa is worshipped at Taputapuātea.

sites.deityNote: The marae that anchored the voyaging triangle — canoes were dedicated here before the long passages. ʻOro, its war god, is not yet in the lexicon; Taʻaroa of the deep is Tangaroa.
sites.summary: The marae of the great voyaging ancestors on Raiatea: the stone courtyard where the god ‘Oro was served and twin-hulled canoes were consecrated before crossing the Pacific. From here the Polynesian triangle was settled.

sites.name: Mauna Kea

deities.depiction: poliahu is worshipped at Mauna Kea.

sites.deityNote: Mauna a Wākea — the mountain of the sky father, where the umbilical cord of the islands was buried. Wākea is not yet in the lexicon.
sources: Hawaiian traditional knowledge; DLNR conservation records
sites.summary: The white mountain, Mauna a Wākea — the summit where sky-father meets earth-mother in Hawaiian cosmology. Highest island peak on earth, its cinder cones hold the oldest shrines of the archipelago.

sites.name: Rano Raraku — Moai Quarry

deities.depiction: The quarry where the moai were born — under Makemake, the creator who made humanity from a bird-man's egg at Orongo.

sites.summary: The quarry of the moai, where nearly four hundred unfinished ancestors still stand buried to their shoulders. Here the statues were born of tuff, and the descent-god Makemake received the birdman cult of Orongo.

sites.name: Uluru
sites.deityNote: Sacred to the Aṉangu. The specific beings of its stories are restricted men's and women's knowledge, not ours to publish — this atlas honours the restriction.

images.title: Petermann Ranges (AU), Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park, Uluru, Kuniya Walk -- 2019 -- 3674
Petermann Ranges (AU), Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park, Uluru, Kuniya Walk -- 2019 -- 3651

sites.summary: The great red monolith of the Aŋyitinja, whose every face carries a Tjukurpa trail — ancestral law written in fissures, caves and waterholes. Climbing it is closed now; the law of the Anangu governs the rock.

sites.name: Ubirr Rock Art
sites.deityNote: Forty thousand years of painting in one gallery — the Rainbow Serpent's oldest images live here; the Rainbow Serpent is not yet in the lexicon.

images.title: Kakadu (AU), Kakadu National Park, Ubirr Rock Art -- 2019 -- 4171
Kakadu (AU), Kakadu National Park, Ubirr Rock Art -- 2019 -- 4169

sites.summary: The gallery rock of Kakadu: x-ray paintings of fish, turtles and the Rainbow Serpent cover its walls, some refreshed for ten thousand years. At the top, the stone country unfolds exactly as the ancestors shaped it.

sites.name: Budj Bim Cultural Landscape
sites.deityNote: The oldest aquaculture on Earth — Gunditjmara-engineered eel channels older than the pyramids, still in the story of the landscape serpent.

images.title: Budj Bim ‐ Mt Eccles National Park, Victoria, Australia 02
Budj Bim ‐ Mt Eccles National Park, Victoria, Australia 39

sites.summary: The engineered wetlands of the Gunditjmara — channels, weirs and ponds built to farm eels, among the oldest aquaculture systems on earth, and a living demonstration of lore-driven land management.

sites.name: Samseonggung Shrine

deities.depiction: The shrine of the three — Hwanin of heaven, Hwanung of the mountain, and Dangun, the bear-son who founded Korea.

sites.summary: The shrine of the Three Sages — Hwanin, Hwanung and Dangun — on Korea’s sacred mountain Kaya: the founding genealogy of the Korean people honoured with shamanic rites that predate Buddhism’s arrival.

sites.name: Seokguram Grotto

deities.depiction: The granite grotto facing the sea — Śākyamuni touches the earth in the pose of the awakening, encircled by bodhisattvas carved from a single granite dome.

sites.summary: The granite grotto of Seokguram, built by the Silla kingdom in the eighth century: a domed rotunda where a serene Buddha faces the sunrise across the East Sea — geometry, water and stone conspiring in a single axis.

sites.name: Jongmyo Shrine
sites.deityNote: The royal ancestral shrine — Korea's kings honoured as spirits, the oldest Confucian royal rite still performed.
sites.summary: The royal shrine of the Choson dynasty, where the spirit-tablets of kings and queens receive the oldest continuously performed court ritual music on earth — Jongmyo Jeryeak, an offering in sound for five centuries.

sites.name: Cerro Ñielol
sites.deityNote: The sacred hill at the heart of Mapuche Temuco — treaty-signed ground beneath native forest, still honoured.

images.title: Temuco, Chile, viewed from the Cerro Ñielol Natural Monument - 200609

sources: Corporación Cerro Ñielol; Treaty of Tapihue site tradition
sites.summary: The sacred hill of the Mapuche in Temuco: a protected forest where the spirits of ancestors are said to walk, and where the Nagche people keep counsel to this day.

sites.name: Villarrica Volcano
sites.deityNote: Ruka Pillán — 'the house of the Pillán', the thunder spirits. The Mapuche name is older than the Spanish volcano.
sites.summary: Villarrica — Ruka Pillán, the house of the spirit of fire: the Mapuche volcano where the mountain’s owner must be honoured before ascent. Its smoking crater remains a living altar of the oldest Chilean theology.

sites.name: Kernavė

deities.depiction: The last pagan capital's sacred groves — Lithuania kept its oaks and its thunder god until 1387, and Kernavė's hillforts remember.

sites.summary: The five mounds of Kernavė, Lithuania’s first capital: hill-fort necropolises on the Neris where the grand dukes of the Palemonid line were burned in horse-and-armour graves before the move to Vilnius.

sites.name: Mount Olympus

deities.depiction: The mountain of the gods — Mytikas at 2,917 m was the first Greek peak climbed for its own myth; the gods' city was always above the weather, which is why no one found it.

sites.summary: Mount Olympus, the seat of the Twelve: Zeus’ thunderbolt, Hera’s throne, the gates of the cloud-gatherer. Mytikas, its highest peak, was the first place in Greece where humans set foot believing gods stood there first.

sites.name: Necromanteion of Acheron

deities.depiction: Oracle of the dead on the banks of the Acheron near ancient Ephyra in Epirus, identified by its excavators with the place where Odysseus summoned the shades in Odyssey 11. The Hellenistic complex, with its subterranean maze of corridors descending to the central hall, is the only Greek sanctuary known to have been built for necromancy proper — though some scholars dispute the identification and read the building as a fortified residence. The site ties the real Acheron valley to the river Achérōn of the underworld passages.

sites.name: Saqqara — Memphite Necropolis

deities.depiction: The necropolis of Memphis and the domain of Sokar, whose image was dragged around its desert sanctuary in the annual festival; the Serapeum galleries here held the buried Apis bulls, the animal substrate of Serapis. The Ptah-Sokar fusion makes the plateau the oldest continuously holy ground in Egypt.

sites.name: Bubastis — Tell Basta

deities.depiction: Per-Bastet, the 'Domain of Bastet' on the Pelusiac branch of the Nile, whose red-granite temple Herodotus called the loveliest in Egypt and whose festival drew what he claimed were seven hundred thousand revellers by river — the capital of the cat-goddess's cult.

sites.name: Sais — Sa el-Hagar

deities.depiction: The western-Delta seat of Neith, 'House of the Bee', where Plato says Solon heard the Atlantis story and where the Twenty-sixth dynasty pharaohs — buried, Herodotus marveled, within the temple precinct — made her cult the theology of an empire.

sites.name: Buto — Tell el-Fara'in

deities.depiction: Per-Wadjet, the ancient twin town of Pe and Dep in the northern Delta and the cobra-goddess's chief cult centre — the place where, in Egyptian memory, the infant Horus was hidden and where the Predynastic 'Buto culture' takes its name.

sites.name: Serapeum of Alexandria

deities.depiction: The acropolis temple that made Serapis a god of the whole Mediterranean: Ptolemy III's great sanctuary, an annex of the Library in its vaults, destroyed in 391 CE — the single most consequential religious building of the Greco-Egyptian age.

sites.summary: The acropolis temple that made Serapis a god of the whole Mediterranean: Ptolemy III's great sanctuary, an annex of the Library in its vaults, destroyed in 391 CE — the single most consequential religious building of the Greco-Egyptian age.

sites.name: Medinet Madi — Narmuthis

deities.depiction: The rare Middle Kingdom temple of Renenutet in the southwestern Faiyum, founded under Amenemhat III and IV in dark sandstone and expanded through the Greco-Roman period — the fixed point of the harvest-goddess's archaeology, set among the vineyards it protects.

sites.name: Mazu Ancestral Temple, Meizhou Island

deities.depiction: The founding temple of the Mazu cult on the island of her birth, off the Fujian coast — rebuilt and enlarged from Song times onward; focal point of the 'Mazu belief and customs' tradition inscribed by UNESCO in 2009. Coordinates are approximate (island-scale).

sites.name: Shaolin Monastery, Mount Song

deities.depiction: The monastery where tradition seats Bodhidharma facing a wall for nine years, and where the martial arts that bear his legend took shape; part of the UNESCO-listed Historic Monuments of Dengfeng in the 'Centre of Heaven and Earth'.

sites.summary: The monastery where tradition seats Bodhidharma facing a wall for nine years, and where the martial arts that bear his legend took shape; part of the UNESCO-listed Historic Monuments of Dengfeng in the 'Centre of Heaven and Earth'.

sites.name: Nippur — The Ekur, Enlil's Mountain House

deities.depiction: Tell Nuffar in southern Iraq, excavated by the University of Pennsylvania (1889–1900) and later Iraqi teams; its scribal quarter yielded tens of thousands of tablets. The mud-brick Ekur ziggurat was Enlil's chief temple and the theological center of Sumer — the place where kingship was believed to be bestowed and his consort Ninlil shared the Tummal precinct.

sites.name: Babylon — Esagila, Marduk's Temple

deities.depiction: The great temple complex of Marduk in ancient Babylon, seat of the akītu New Year festival at which the Enūma eliš was recited before the assembled gods. Its ziggurat, Etemenanki, is the monument behind the later Tower of Babel tradition.

sites.name: Aššur — Qal'at Sherqat

deities.depiction: UNESCO-listed ruins of the first Assyrian royal capital on a bluff above the Tigris. The Aššur temple — the god's house bearing the god's own name — crowned the citadel and was rebuilt by nearly every great Assyrian king from Shalmaneser I to Ashurbanipal.

sites.name: Uruk — The Anu Ziggurat and White Temple

deities.depiction: The 'White Temple' of the Late Uruk period (c. 3500–3350 BCE) atop the Anu ziggurat in Uruk's Anu district — among the oldest monumental temple platforms known, dedicated to the sky god Anu and contemporary with the invention of writing at the same city.

sites.name: Sanctuary of Diana Nemorensis, Lake Nemi

deities.depiction: The terraced sanctuary of Diana of the Wood on the rim of a volcanic crater lake in the Alban Hills — the grove of the rex Nemorensis, whose priest won office by slaying his predecessor, and a precinct rich in votive terracotta wombs and limbs. The lake itself, speculum Dianae, reflected the goddess; Caligula's pleasure barges, raised in 1929–32 and burned in 1944, made it the founding drama of underwater archaeology.

sites.name: Kildare (Cill Dara) — Brigid's Fire Temple

deities.depiction: The monastic site founded at the oak wood (cell dara) where St Brigid's double monastery kept a perpetual flame tended by nineteen nuns — a fire-cult continuity with the goddess Brigid that Irish tradition itself insisted on, whatever the historical joins. The flame was suppressed in the sixteenth century and rekindled in 1993; the twelfth-century cathedral and holy well complete a cult landscape straddling goddess and saint.

sites.name: South Barrule, Isle of Man

deities.depiction: The mountain the Manx ballad tradition names as Manannán's throne — the sea-lord's seat from which he shrouded the island in mist against pirates and levied his yearly tribute of rushes. sites.name: Rathcroghan (Rath Cruachan), Co. Roscommon
